and the SUVIMAX study found a reduction of total cancer incidence in men but not women with low dose vitamin E along
with vitamin C, b-carotene, selenium, and zinc. Two smaller, short-term intervention studies found no effect of a-tocopherol
supplementation on mammary dysplasia or benign breast disease. Several trials have also been unable to demonstrate a protective
effect of vitamin E supplementation on the risk or recurrence of colorectal adenomatous polyps.
Selenium
A few trials have suggested that selenium supplementation may have a protective effect on liver cancer in high-risk groups living in
low-selenium areas. For example, the provision of selenium-fortiﬁed salt to a town in Qidong, China, with high rates of primary
liver cancer, reduced the incidence of this cancer by 35% compared with towns that did not receive this intervention. Some trials
have also demonstrated the incidence of liver cancer to be signiﬁcantly reduced in subjects with hepatitis B and among members of
families with a history of liver cancer receiving a daily supplement of 200 mg of selenium for 4 and 2 years, respectively. The Nutri-
tional Prevention of Cancer Trial (NPCT) in the US also supported a possible protective role of selenium in 1312 patients (mostly
